title: the birth
hook: a wedding procession, a brother driving the bride's chariot, and a voice from the sky that turns him into a killer
carry: a promise made at sword point

segments.voice: Yesterday the Mahabharata serial ended: Yudhishthira chose to stand in the dark beside his family. Your line was he will stay in hell. Today a new book opens, the Bhagavata Purana, and a new story: Krishna as a child.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY ENDS.` · `A NEW BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: The wedding is over and the music is still playing. Devaki, a princess of the Yadu clan, has just married Vasudeva. Her cousin Kamsa, a prince of Mathura, wants to honor her, so he takes the reins and drives the bridal chariot himself. Conches, drums, gifts of horses and elephants. A happy brother on a happy day. Then, the Bhagavata says, a voice speaks out of the sky, without a body, straight at the driver. Fool. The eighth child of the woman you are driving will kill you.
screen: `A WEDDING CHARIOT.` → `KAMSA HOLDS THE REINS.` → `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Kamsa grabs his cousin by the hair and draws his sword. The procession stops dead. And here is the first surprise: Vasudeva doesn't fight. He talks, gently. Death comes to everyone who is born, he says, today or in a hundred years. Killing a woman, your own sister, on her wedding day won't change that. It will only stain you. Kamsa won't listen. So Vasudeva thinks fast and makes a terrible bargain to save his wife's life right now. I'll bring you every son she bears. They're the danger, not her. Kamsa knows Vasudeva keeps his word, and he lowers the sword. And Vasudeva does keep it. When their first son is born, he carries the baby to Kamsa himself, and the text praises him: a man who holds to truth even when it costs everything. For a moment Kamsa is moved. Only the eighth child is my danger, he says; take this one home. The mercy doesn't last. The sage Narada visits Kamsa and stirs up his fear, and Kamsa locks Devaki and Vasudeva in a prison and begins to kill their children. So Krishna's story begins not with a cradle but with a promise made at sword point, and a father who keeps it. The book that will be full of a child's laughter starts in a prison cell.
screen: `THE SWORD COMES OUT` · `VASUDEVA REASONS WITH KAMSA` · `"I'LL BRING YOU EVERY SON"` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT, A PRISON CELL`

segments.voice: Vasudeva's first move was not to fight but to speak calmly to someone with a sword out. Bring to mind one tense conversation you might face, and as you breathe, picture yourself staying steady in it; you don't need the right words yet. If you pray, you can ask in your own way for a calm voice.
The birth. Krishna's story starts before he is born, with a voice at a wedding and a promise Vasudeva keeps.
Your line: a promise made at sword point. Vasudeva's word held, even when it cost everything. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The story of Krishna's birth is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana; Hindus hear it in recitations and festival retellings, especially around Krishna Janmashtami.

chat.says: Why did Vasudeva promise to give his babies to Kamsa?
options: To save Devaki's life right then, since Kamsa had his sword out at her.
Because he agreed with Kamsa that the babies were a danger to Mathura.
Because the voice from the sky told him he had to hand them over.
chat.meaning: Kamsa had drawn his sword on Devaki. Promising every son saved her life, and Vasudeva kept his word.

Kamsa.meaning: a prince of Mathura who fears Devaki's eighth child

notes: All paraphrase; the voice's words and the dialogue are glosses, not quotations from any translation.
Vasudeva's 'today or in a hundred years' follows the Bhagavata's own wording of his argument (10.1.38); confirm.

Confirm in 10.1: Kamsa drives the chariot out of affection; the bodiless voice names the eighth child; Vasudeva's argument that death is certain for the born; Kamsa's release of the first son (Kirtiman); Narada's visit prompting imprisonment.
Kamsa is called Devaki's cousin (he is the son of Ugrasena, she the daughter of Devaka, Ugrasena's brother); the text often calls her his sister. Confirm preferred wording.
